64.title: Not-self, taught
64.hook: to the five: is the body you, is feeling, is any of the five heaps mine (SN 22.59)
64.howItsDone: In many Buddhist traditions, practitioners reflect on the five aggregates in meditation, noting of each 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self', and the Anattalakkhana Sutta is chanted in Theravada monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kondañña sees: the first of the five understood that whatever arises, ends. Your line was it arises, it ends. What mood did you watch come and go? Day sixty-four, and a new week: the sangha grows.

Try this. Tell someone who you are in one sentence. Most of us reach for the same things. My body. My job. My feelings about things. My memories, my opinions, my personality. That's me. A few days after the first sermon, all five companions have now understood the basics, and the Buddha sits them down in the Deer Park again. This time he goes after that one sentence. He takes the pieces we point to when we say me, and holds each one up to the light, and asks a very simple question about it. It's the second teaching in the old accounts, and today's word.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU, IN ONE SENTENCE?` → `THE PIECES WE CALL ME.` → `ONE SIMPLE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Not-self. In Pali, anatta. The teaching is called the Discourse on the Characteristic of Not-self, and it works like a careful conversation. First the Buddha names five heaps, the five bundles that make up a person as we experience one: the body; feeling, meaning pleasant, unpleasant or neither; perception, recognizing things; mental formations, our urges and habits; and consciousness, the knowing. Then he asks about the body. If the body were really your self, it wouldn't lead to trouble, and you could just say: let my body be like this, don't let it be like that. But you can't. It gets sick. It ages. It doesn't take orders. Is the body permanent or impermanent, he asks. Impermanent, they say. And is something impermanent a source of lasting ease, or of unease? Unease. Then is it right to look at it and say, this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, they say. He asks the same thing of feeling, then perception, then formations, then consciousness. Same answers every time. The texts say that as the five heard this, their minds were freed. Two things are worth knowing about this. First, it's a practice more than a philosophy. You look at a feeling and ask, is this me, is this mine? The looking is the point. Second, Buddhist schools have argued for centuries over exactly what it means. Most teachers say it doesn't mean you don't exist. Your body, your moods, your thoughts are all really happening. The teaching is that none of them is a fixed owner sitting in the middle, holding the others. There's no one piece you could point to and say, that, forever, is me.
screen: `FIVE HEAPS MAKE A PERSON.` · `IS IT PERMANENT? IS IT MINE?` · `THE SAME QUESTION, FIVE TIMES.` · `NOT 'YOU DON'T EXIST.'` · then, large: `NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask of one feeling, is this me? Settle, and breathe. Notice whatever feeling is here right now. Tiredness, worry, a little boredom, contentment. Find it in the body if you can. Then ask it, gently: are you me? Did I choose you? Will you stay? Watch it while you ask. There's no answer to get right. Just notice what happens to a feeling when you stop assuming it's you. The bell holds the time.
Not-self. Anatta: no body, feeling, perception, habit or knowing that you can hold up and say, this, forever, is mine.
Your line: not mine. Today, when a hard feeling grabs you, try saying quietly, this feeling is here, but it's not mine to keep. Day sixty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: a claim that you don't really exist.
what it means: a way of looking at body, feelings and thoughts and seeing that none of them is a fixed, owned self.

65.title: Yasa's night
65.hook: a rich young man wakes after a party, sickened, and walks out into the night (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)
65.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Yasa's story as one of the first conversions after the Deer Park, and remember his father as the first lay follower to take refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, as lay Buddhists still do today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not-self: five heaps, and none of them a fixed owner. Your line was not mine. Which feeling did you ask, is this me? Day sixty-five.

It's three in the morning. The party's over but nobody went home. There are people asleep on the couch, on the floor, someone snoring with a hand still around a cup. The music stopped a while ago. And you're the only one awake, looking at it all, and something turns in your stomach that isn't the food. Maybe you know that feeling. A young man named Yasa knew it. He was the son of a very rich family in Benares, with a house for every season and musicians who played for him through the night. One night he woke up before everyone else. And what he did next is today's story.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE ONLY ONE AWAKE.` → `A RICH YOUNG MAN NAMED YASA.`

segments.voice: The old monastic rulebook, the Vinaya, tells it vividly. Yasa wakes, and the lamps are still burning, and he sees the musicians and attendants asleep around him, sprawled in every direction, mouths open, instruments dropped. The text says it looked to him like a cemetery. And he cries out: how distressing this is, how oppressive. He puts on his golden slippers and walks out of the house, out of the city gate, into the dark. His feet take him toward the Deer Park. And the Buddha, the story says, is walking up and down in the open air before dawn. He hears Yasa's cry, and answers: this is not distressing, this is not oppressive. Come, Yasa, sit down. I'll teach you. So a young man in party clothes and golden slippers sits down on the ground with a wandering teacher, and listens, and something in him settles. Now, why does this story matter? Notice how much it sounds like another one. A young man of a rich family. Pleasure all around him. A night when he looks at sleeping bodies and sees the truth under the glitter. A walk out into the dark. That's the Buddha's own story, his great going forth. Yasa lives it in one night, and this time there's someone waiting on the road. And look at his name. Yasa means fame, or glory. The man named Fame found the party empty. The story doesn't stop at one person, either. His father comes searching, following the tracks of those golden slippers, and becomes the first lay follower to take the three refuges. His mother and his former wife become the first women lay followers. And Yasa's friends come looking for him too. Tomorrow, where that leads.
screen: `IT LOOKED LIKE A CEMETERY.` · `COME, YASA, SIT DOWN.` · `THE BUDDHA'S STORY IN ONE NIGHT.` · `HIS FAMILY FOLLOWS THE SLIPPERS.` · then, large: `WALK OUT OF THE PARTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing that has lost its shine. Settle and breathe. Think of something you keep doing that doesn't give you what it used to. An app you open without meaning to. A habit that's gone flat. A place you keep going because you always have. Picture it the way Yasa saw that room, with the lamps still on. You don't have to hate it. Just see it clearly, and imagine standing up and walking out the door. The bell holds the time.
Yasa's night. A rich young man wakes after a party, sees it clearly, walks out into the dark, and finds the Buddha on the road.
Your line: walk out of the party. Today, leave one thing early that has lost its shine, a scroll, a conversation, a habit, and see where your feet go. Day sixty-five.

66.title: Sixty sent out
66.hook: wander for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.11)
66.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics in many countries still walk for alms each morning, and the phrase 'for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many' (bahujana hitaya, bahujana sukhaya) is widely quoted as a motto for teaching and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasa's night: golden slippers, a party that looked like a cemetery, and a walk into the dark. Your line was walk out of the party. What did you leave early? Day sixty-six.

Picture the first time you told a friend about something that really helped you. A book, a song, a way of getting through a bad week. You couldn't keep it to yourself. Now picture the Deer Park a few weeks after Yasa's night. Yasa's friends have come looking for him, first four, then fifty more, and they've stayed. With the five companions and Yasa, the texts count sixty people who now understand what the Buddha understood. Sixty, in a grove near Benares. Plenty of teachers would keep a group like that close. Build a school. Stay together. Instead, the Buddha gathers them and sends them all away.
screen: `YOU COULDN'T KEEP IT TO YOURSELF.` → `SIXTY IN A GROVE.` → `HE SENDS THEM ALL AWAY.`

segments.voice: What he tells them is one of the most loved passages in the monastic texts. Go, monks, and wander, for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit and happiness of gods and humans. And then a small instruction that's easy to miss: don't two of you go the same way. Scatter. Sixty roads instead of one. Teach something, he says, that's good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end. There are people with only a little dust in their eyes, and if they don't hear it, they'll miss it. There are three things worth noticing. The first is the reason he gives. Not for my glory, not to win an argument, not to fill a hall. For the good of the many. For their happiness. Compassion is the engine. The second is the method: walking. In Pali this is carika, wandering from place to place on foot. For centuries afterward, monks and nuns walked, and in many places they still walk for alms each morning. The teaching spread at the speed of feet. The third is that the Buddha doesn't stay behind to wait for results. He says he'll go too, back toward Uruvela, near the tree where he woke up. Nobody is left in charge of the grove. And one honest note: the texts give us the send-off, but they don't follow all sixty. We know where a few of them went. Most of their roads are lost. What survives is the instruction, and the reason: the good of the many.
screen: `FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.` · `DON'T TWO GO THE SAME WAY.` · `CARIKA: WANDERING ON FOOT.` · `MOST OF THEIR ROADS ARE LOST.` · then, large: `FOR THE HAPPINESS OF THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing for a stranger, starting in your mind. Settle and breathe. Think of the people you'll pass today whose names you'll never know. The person at the register. A driver. Someone in the elevator. Pick one, even a face you haven't met yet. Wish them something simple: may your day be a little easier. Then think of one small good you could actually do for them. Hold the door. Say thank you like you mean it. The bell holds the time.
Sixty sent out. The first sixty who understood, sent walking on separate roads, for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many.
Your line: for the good of many. Today, do one kind thing for someone who can't thank you, and go your own way afterward. Day sixty-six.

67.title: The fire sermon
67.hook: to a thousand fire-worshipers: all is burning, with greed, hate and delusion (SN 35.28)
67.howItsDone: The Fire Sermon (Adittapariyaya Sutta) is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and its image of greed, hatred and delusion as three fires is one of the most common ways Buddhist teachers explain what nibbana cools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sixty sent out, each on a separate road. Your line was for the good of many. Who got your one small kindness? Day sixty-seven.

Everyone knows how to talk to their own crowd. Musicians talk about songs. Coaches talk in plays. The Buddha has walked back to Uruvela, near the tree of his awakening, and there he meets three brothers named Kassapa. They're famous teachers with matted hair, and with their followers they number about a thousand. Their whole religious life is tending sacred fires, keeping the flames going, making offerings into them. The old texts tell of wonders and long nights before the brothers are won over, and then they throw their hair and their fire tools into the river. Afterward he leads all thousand up a hill called Gaya Head, looking out over the land. And to people who have spent their lives watching fire, he talks about fire.
screen: `TALK TO YOUR OWN CROWD.` → `A THOUSAND WHO TENDED FIRES.` → `UP THE HILL AT GAYA HEAD.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the texts, with one stark sentence: everything, monks, is burning. And what is burning? The eye is burning. What the eye sees is burning. The seeing itself is burning. The ear, and sounds. The nose, and smells. The tongue, the body, the mind, and everything they touch. Burning with what? With the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. Burning with birth, aging and death, with sorrow and grief and despair. Imagine hearing that as a fire-keeper. You've fed flames every day of your life, and now someone points at your own eyes and says: there's the fire. You don't have to climb a hill to find it. It's in the wanting, in the anger, in the confusion. And then the turn. Someone who sees this, he says, grows tired of feeding it. They become disenchanted, and cool. The wanting fades, and with its fading, they are free. The texts say that as they listened, the thousand were freed too. Here's something to repeat to a friend tonight. That cooling has a name you already know. Nibbana, nirvana, is often explained as the going out of a flame, the way a lamp goes out when the oil is used up. The fire sermon is where that picture burns brightest. And it traveled a long way. In 1922, the poet T. S. Eliot named a whole section of The Waste Land The Fire Sermon, and ended it with the word burning, over and over. A talk on a hill in India turned up in a famous poem in English.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS BURNING.` · `GREED, HATRED, DELUSION.` · `SEE IT, AND IT COOLS.` · `A SERMON IN A MODERN POEM.` · then, large: `ALL IS BURNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you are burning. Settle and breathe. Scan yourself slowly, like you're checking a house for heat. Is there wanting somewhere, pulling you toward a screen, a snack, a person? Is there irritation, a hot spot about something someone said? Is there fog, a place you'd rather not look at? Don't fight any of it. Just find the warm places, and name them: wanting, anger, fog. Then breathe out slowly, as if you were cooling soup. The bell holds the time.
The fire sermon. Taught to a thousand fire-keepers on Gaya Head: the senses burn with greed, hatred and delusion, and seeing it lets them cool.
Your line: all is burning. Today, when you feel heat rise, wanting or anger, name the fire, and take one cooling breath before you feed it. Day sixty-seven.

68.title: Sariputta and Moggallana
68.hook: Assaji's short verse: things arise from a cause, and the Buddha tells their cause; Sariputta understands at once
68.howItsDone: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples, often shown standing on either side of him in temples, and Assaji's verse, 'ye dhamma hetuppabhava', is still chanted and has been inscribed on stupas, seals and images across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fire sermon on Gaya Head: greed, hatred and delusion, burning. Your line was all is burning. Where did you catch the heat, and cool it? Day sixty-eight.

Two best friends make a pact. Whoever finds the answer first, tells the other. That's the whole deal. Their names are Upatissa and Kolita, and they grew up together, sons of important families near the city of Rajagaha. As young men they went to a festival, looked at the crowds laughing and the actors on stage, and both thought the same thing: in a hundred years, none of these people will be alive. So they left home together to search for what doesn't die. They studied with a famous teacher, learned everything he had, and it wasn't enough. So they made the pact. Then one morning, in the streets of Rajagaha, Upatissa sees a monk walking for alms.
screen: `WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST, TELLS.` → `A HUNDRED YEARS FROM NOW.` → `A MONK IN THE STREET.`

segments.voice: The monk is Assaji, one of the five from the Deer Park. What catches Upatissa's eye isn't anything he says. It's the way he walks: calm, collected, eyes down, every movement settled. Upatissa follows him and waits politely until he's finished his meal. Then he asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji is honest. I'm new, he says. I can't explain the teaching at length. But I can tell you the gist. And he says a single verse, four short lines. In paraphrase: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and also how they cease. That's the teaching of the great one. That's all. And the texts say that hearing it, Upatissa's dhamma eye opened, the same clear seeing Kondañña had: whatever arises, ceases. He runs to Kolita. Kolita sees his face and knows at once. Did you find it? Upatissa repeats the verse, and Kolita understands too. The pact is kept. They go to the Buddha together, and bring many of their old teacher's students with them. Upatissa becomes known as Sariputta, son of Sari, his mother's name. Kolita becomes Moggallana. They become the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta known for wisdom, Moggallana for deep meditation powers. Now here's the thing to tell someone tonight. That little verse, in Pali ye dhamma hetuppabhava, became one of the most copied lines in the Buddhist world. It's been found carved on stones, stamped on clay seals, and set inside statues and stupas across Asia, as a summary of the whole teaching. The Dhammapada says one word of sense, which brings peace to the hearer, is better than a thousand empty ones. Sometimes one verse is enough.
screen: `THE WAY ASSAJI WALKED.` · `I CAN ONLY GIVE THE GIST.` · `THE PACT IS KEPT.` · `ONE VERSE, CARVED ACROSS ASIA.` · then, large: `ONE VERSE WAS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass on one good line. Settle and breathe. Think back over what's helped you, here or anywhere. A saying, a verse, a sentence someone once said to you at the right moment. Pick just one. Say it silently a few times, and feel why it helped. Then think of one person who might need it this week. Not a lecture. Not a long explanation. Just the line, the way Assaji gave it. The bell holds the time.
Sariputta and Moggallana. Two friends who kept their pact, and became the Buddha's chief disciples, after one short verse from Assaji.
Your line: one verse was enough. Today, send one good line to someone who might need it, no explanation attached. Day sixty-eight.

69.title: Coming home
69.hook: he returns to Kapilavatthu; young Rahula asks for his inheritance and is given the teaching
69.howItsDone: In many Theravada countries boys ordain for a time as novices, following Rahula as the first, and monasteries require parents' permission before a child is ordained, a rule traced to King Suddhodana's request.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputta and Moggallana: two friends, one pact, and Assaji's four-line verse. Your line was one verse was enough. Who got your good line? Day sixty-nine.

Going home after a long time away is its own kind of nervous. The streets look smaller. Everyone knows the old you. Remember the night Siddhartha left Kapilavatthu, the palace, his wife Yasodhara asleep, their newborn son Rahula beside her. He didn't wake them. Now, years later, word reaches his father, King Suddhodana, that his son has become a famous teacher. The king sends messengers begging him to visit. And he comes. But not the way a prince comes home. He walks into his hometown with a crowd of monks, and in the morning he does what monks do. He goes from house to house along the streets, with a bowl, asking for food.
screen: `THE STREETS LOOK SMALLER.` → `THE KING SENDS FOR HIM.` → `A PRINCE WITH A BOWL.`

segments.voice: Later tradition fills in the scene. The king is mortified. My son, begging, in my own city? Our family has never done this. The Buddha answers that his family now is the line of Buddhas before him, and this is their custom. Then comes the moment the old monastic texts do record. Rahula is about seven now. His mother, Yasodhara, sends him to his father with a message. Go and ask him for your inheritance. So a small boy walks up to the teacher everyone's talking about, stands close, and the texts say he told him, pleasant is your shadow, monk. Then, when the Buddha gets up and walks away, Rahula follows him, saying: give me my inheritance, monk. Give me my inheritance. And here's the Buddha's answer. He doesn't hand over land, or gold, or a crown. He turns to Sariputta, the wise friend from yesterday, and asks him to ordain the boy. Rahula becomes the first novice, a young monk in training. The reasoning, as the commentaries tell it: the wealth he's asking for brings trouble and ends. I'll give him an inheritance that doesn't. The texts are honest that this hurt. King Suddhodana, who had already lost his son to the road, now loses his grandson too. He goes to the Buddha and says: when my son left, it was pain. When his son left, it was pain again. Please, don't let children be ordained without their parents' permission. And the Buddha agrees, and makes it a rule. Buddhist monasteries still keep it: a child needs a parent's consent. So one family's grief became a kindness for every family after.
screen: `A PRINCE WITH A BOWL.` · `GIVE ME MY INHERITANCE.` · `THE BOY IS GIVEN THE TEACHING.` · `A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.` · then, large: `THE REAL INHERITANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone something that lasts. Settle and breathe. Think of what you've inherited that wasn't money. A way your grandmother laughed. How your father fixed things. A saying, a recipe, a habit of patience. Let one come to mind, and feel it for a moment. Then think of someone younger, a child, a niece, a new coworker. What's one thing you could pass on to them that no one could take away? The bell holds the time.
Coming home. The Buddha returns to Kapilavatthu with a bowl, and his son Rahula, asking for an inheritance, is given the teaching.
Your line: the real inheritance. Today, pass on one thing that can't be bought, a skill, a story, a kindness, to someone who'll outlast you. Day sixty-nine.

70.title: The women ask
70.hook: Mahapajapati and many women shave their heads and walk to ask for ordination; Ananda speaks for them
70.tomorrow: the man with the finger garland
70.howItsDone: Buddhist nuns live in monastic communities in many countries; fully ordained bhikkhunis are found especially in Chinese, Korean, Taiwanese and Vietnamese traditions, and in growing but debated numbers in Theravada countries, while many Buddhist women also live as novices or precept-holding renunciants.

segments.voice: Yesterday, coming home: Rahula asked for his inheritance and was given the teaching. Your line was the real inheritance. What did you pass on? Day seventy.

Think of a woman you know who had to ask twice for something a man got by asking once. Maybe more than twice. Hold her in mind. Mahapajapati Gotami was the Buddha's aunt. When his mother died a week after his birth, she raised him as her own. Years later, in Kapilavatthu, she came to him and asked: let women go forth too, into the homeless life, as nuns. And he said no. She asked again. No. A third time. No. She went away weeping. But she didn't stop. When he left for the city of Vesali, a long way off, she cut off her hair, put on the ochre robes, and set out walking after him. And she didn't go alone.
screen: `A WOMAN WHO ASKED TWICE.` → `THE AUNT WHO RAISED HIM.` → `NO, NO, NO.` → `SHE SETS OUT WALKING.`

segments.voice: Many women of the Sakya clan walk with her, heads shaved, robed. When they reach Vesali, the old text describes her standing outside the gate of the hall: feet swollen, body covered in dust, in tears. Ananda, the Buddha's cousin and attendant, finds her there and asks what's wrong. She tells him. So Ananda goes in and asks for them. The answer is no, three times. Then Ananda tries a different question. Lord, are women able, if they go forth, to reach the fruits of the path, all the way to full awakening? And the Buddha answers: yes, Ananda, they are. Ananda presses on: then think of Mahapajapati, who nursed you, fed you her own milk when your mother died. And the Buddha agrees. Women may be ordained. Today's word is what they became: bhikkhuni, a fully ordained Buddhist nun. It's the feminine of bhikkhu, monk, and at its root it means one who lives on alms. The texts also say women were given eight extra rules, placing nuns under the monks in certain ways. Scholars and Buddhists today discuss those rules, and their history, seriously and with care. And what happened to the order afterward differs by place. Full ordination for nuns continued unbroken in Chinese, Korean, Taiwanese and Vietnamese communities. In Theravada countries it died out many centuries ago; since the late twentieth century, some have revived it, and others in those traditions do not accept the revival. In Tibetan communities, full ordination for women has long been debated. Meanwhile, the first nuns left something extraordinary: the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. It's one of the oldest collections of poems by women anywhere in the world. Now, this week: not-self, Yasa's night, sixty sent out, the fire sermon, two friends and one verse, coming home, and today, the women who walked.
screen: `FEET SWOLLEN, COVERED IN DUST.` · `ARE WOMEN ABLE? YES.` · `BHIKKHUNI, A NUN.` · `THE THERIGATHA, THEIR POEMS.` · then, large: `THEY WALKED BAREFOOT TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a woman who had to ask twice. Settle and breathe. Bring back the woman you thought of at the start. A mother, a teacher, a friend, a grandmother, maybe yourself. Picture her standing at a door she had to knock on more than once. Notice the dust on her feet. Then, silently, thank her for not stopping. If there's a way to tell her today, even a text, hold that thought. The bell holds the time.
Bhikkhuni. A fully ordained Buddhist nun, first opened to women when Mahapajapati and the Sakya women walked to Vesali to ask.
Your line: they walked barefoot to ask. Today, back up someone who has to ask again, the way Ananda did. Day seventy.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. the answer has been no, three times. what do you ask next?
options: nothing. you've done what you could.
whether women are able to reach awakening.
whether the women could go home and try later.
fork.reveal: he asks whether women can reach full awakening. the Buddha says yes. then Ananda reminds him who nursed him. and the answer changes.

original.note: Pali: a nun, feminine of bhikkhu. At its root, one who lives on alms. Sanskrit bhikṣuṇī.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Buddhist word for a female monk.
what it means: a fully ordained nun, an order that began when women walked to Vesali and Ananda spoke for them.

what a scholar hears: Vinaya, Cullavagga 10.1 and AN 8.51; the eight garudhammas and their history are discussed by scholars; the Therigatha is among the oldest surviving collections of women's poetry.
